account: RL-Zero's weight change is small (0.24 % of the weight norm), and under any on-policy reward about 12 % of it sits in 8 input-output pairs per matrix (top-8 share: LM-judge General 0.127, Math 0.118-0.135, imitation-trained Think-SFT 0.030); the inputs are directions the base already drives in any step-by-step text (8-11x a random subspace; code text 0.87 as much as math), so Think-SFT's and Code-RL's changes also overlap them (4.8x chance; Code 5.2x Think-SFT) and Math's per-matrix pattern follows Think-SFT's (rho 0.59), not IF-RL's (-0.01); the output paired with each input is what the reward chose (on code, Code's pairs raise the pass rate 7.0 points over a random edit, Math's 1.5).

The base's later layers enlarge these pairs only when they stay paired (95x a random edit's residual shift), and they act in every sample as a graded reweighting of each token the base already writes, not as a switch between modes: hold-on words go up (+1.1 to +1.7 points of readout positions), wrap-up words go down (-1.4), and the base's own wrong step becomes half as likely; so short answers of the 1x edit are 82.9 % right, m21's quick wrong answers are no more answer-first than the plain base's (0.25 vs 0.21), and the edit is written in full (0.99996 of the intended change).

The effect on outcomes is one multiplier on the reliability of each step, not a preference for RL's own routes: the edit adds right answers where the base finishes wrong (+13.5 points over a second base sample) and where the base never solves the problem in 4 samples (14 % vs 5 %, RL 15 %); at 1.5x, which stands in for the diffuse 88 % of the change it leaves out, it equals RL per sample, under the vote and beyond the base's reach (456 vs 457; 200.25 vs 200.0; vote 216.25 vs 215.92; 0.88 of RL's lift), and it does not carry RL's losses (on code problems RL fails: edit 0.45, base resample 0.44, RL 0.22).

Inference reproduces the part of this reweighting that sits at a single token, the first word of the answer: a plain base answer that already opens deliberatively is as right as a cued one (-0.03), and a three-token cue, a self-chosen 'Okay' or a one-tensor hand edit gives 397-411 of 500, the level of RL step 100 (417.5); step 100 has the cued base's cap-hit rate and +7-point vote gain, writes right answers only 15 % longer (final RL 61 %), and still gains +8.5 of 500 from the cue, because 100 steps install only part of the per-token shift.

Inference gets the per-step reliability only by selecting among whole answers, which works because the base's slips are chance events whose wrong answers split (pairwise agreement 0.26; splitting adds 0.07 to the vote over 4 on MATH-500 and 0.11 on hard328; the problems the vote over 12 gains are split problems, not ties); a T 1.0 plurality over 4-12 samples therefore recovers RL wherever the right answer is already the base's plurality (81 % of the MATH-500 gap lies on problems the base solves at least 1 time in 4; a vote over 6 equals one RL sample), but only if sampling keeps the long right routes, so not at T 0.6, where 52-63 % of answers past 4,096 tokens loop, and not under a 4,096-token cap (71 % of Karpathy's lost hard328 problems).

Where the right answer is rarer than the base's wrong ones, selection has nothing to amplify (the base has no right sample on 26 of the 36 hard328 problems RL's vote wins), so the cued base's vote stays 8.8 points under RL on the 328, while the 1.5x edit, which makes every step more reliable, does not stay under it.

consequences.claim: S2 and S4: by step 100 the per-token hold-on shift is partly in the weights, in every sample. So a step-100 plain sample that does not open deliberatively still deliberates later and is right more often than the untrained plain base's non-deliberative answer to the same problem. But it lacks the first-token part, so it gains less than the full cue gain of about 0.5. A switch account (an unswitched sample is a plain-base answer) gives about 0. An accuracy-only account (every step-100 sample is as good as its average one) gives the full step-100-minus-plain gap of about 0.45-0.55.
consequences.why_new: F07 is pooled over all samples, F51 uses the untrained base only, and F25/F41/F49 measure length, cap hits and the vote. No fact or result compares step-100 samples, split by their opening, with the plain base's answers on the same problems.
consequences.statistic: D = mean over problems of (right rate of the problem's non-deliberative step-100 plain samples minus right of the plain base's T3 answer), as a fraction (0-1)
consequences.rows: MATH-500 problems where the T3 (plain base, T 1.0) answer is non-deliberative and at least 1 of the 4 step-100 plain samples is non-deliberative. Non-deliberative uses the flag rule of result-1f98b0: the first 240 characters hold none of Okay/Hmm/Let me/Let's/Wait/First/Alright before any equation or 'Answer'.
consequences.computation: 1) For each problem, read the v3 grade and the first 240 characters of step-100 plain sample 0 (s0100_plain-01) and samples 1-3 (s0100_plain_s123-01), and T3's grade and opening from t1_t3_items-01/per_problem.json. 2) Flag every answer with the rule. 3) Keep the problems in rows. 4) u_i = right rate of the non-deliberative step-100 samples, t_i = T3 right (0/1); D = mean(u_i - t_i). 5) Resample problems with replacement 10,000 times; the 90 % interval is the 5th-95th percentile of D. 6) Also report the accuracy-only value: mean over the same problems of (right rate of all 4 step-100 plain samples - t_i). If fewer than 50 problems qualify, report undecided.
consequences.null: The switch null (account-1 S2/S4): a step-100 sample that does not open deliberatively is an untrained plain-base answer, so D is about 0 apart from sampling noise.

consequences.claim: S2: Code-RL's pairs at 1x reweight every token, including the hold-on words their late directions share with Math's. So an m21 answer that does not open deliberatively is still right more often than the plain base's non-deliberative answer to the same problem. The gain is part of the cue's ~0.5, not 0 (an unswitched plain-base answer) and not m21's whole gap over the plain base.
consequences.why_new: F11/F12 looked only at m21's quick wrong answers, and F22/F44 at the length of right answers. Account-1/c2 compares m21's own openings with each other against the cued base's difficulty. No fact or result pairs m21's non-deliberative answers with the plain base's non-deliberative answers on the same problems.
consequences.statistic: D_m21 = mean over problems of (m21 right minus T3 right) where both answers are non-deliberative, as a fraction (0-1)
consequences.rows: Problems among the first 250 of MATH-500 where both the m21 completion (base + Code-RL top-8 at 1x, plain, T 1.0) and the T3 answer are non-deliberative by the flag rule of result-1f98b0
consequences.computation: 1) Join the m21 rows to t1_t3_items-01/per_problem.json by problem index. 2) Flag both answers with the rule on their first 240 characters. 3) Keep problems where both are non-deliberative. 4) D_m21 = mean(m21 right - T3 right), v3. 5) Resample problems with replacement 10,000 times; the 90 % interval is the 5th-95th percentile. 6) Also report the accuracy-only value (all m21 rows on the same problems minus T3). If fewer than 50 problems qualify, report undecided.
consequences.null: The switch null: Code's pairs switch some samples fully and leave the rest as plain-base answers, so on problems where both are non-deliberative, m21 is right as often as T3 (D about 0).

consequences.claim: S1 and S2: on-policy RL shares the output side of the deliberation pairs whatever the reward (the late directions that read Okay/Wait are in both RL-Math and RL-Code), while imitation-trained Think-SFT overlaps only the driven inputs. So relative to its own input-side capture, Code-RL 3.1's change sits on Math 3.1's top-8 output side far more than Think-SFT's does. The ratio of ratios removes overall concentration and the rank-8 chance levels.
consequences.why_new: F27 and F46 use cap_right (the input side) only. Account-2/c1 sets Think-SFT against Math 3.0, which has the same reward. No fact or result compares output-side to input-side capture for Code-RL against Think-SFT.
consequences.statistic: Q_C = median over matrices of [cap_left(Code 3.1)/cap_right(Code 3.1)] / [cap_left(Think-SFT)/cap_right(Think-SFT)], all against Math 3.1's top-8 subspaces, unitless
consequences.rows: All 224 layer matrices (32 layers x q, k, v, o, gate, up, down) with cap_left and cap_right for both Code 3.1 and Think-SFT against the Math 3.1 top-8 subspace entry
consequences.computation: 1) For each matrix, read the four capture shares. 2) q = (cap_left_C / cap_right_C) / (cap_left_TS / cap_right_TS); the chance levels 8/d_out and 8/d_in cancel. 3) Q_C = median of q. 4) Resample matrices with replacement 10,000 times; the 90 % interval is the 5th-95th percentile of the median.
consequences.null: Another model's directions: whatever lands in Math 3.1's top-8 subspace lands there equally on both sides, whatever the objective, so Code's output/input ratio equals Think-SFT's (Q_C about 1).

denials.why: Account-2 says the 1.5x edit carries RL's re-ranking of routes, so the edit's wrong answers should be nearer RL's than the base's are. Under S3 the edit and RL lower only the rate of chance slips. Their remaining finished wrong answers are the base's own systematic misreadings, plus slips that split. With each model's agreement normalized by its own concentration, the slip fraction cancels and N(E,R) equals N(B,R).
denials.instead: S3 (one reliability multiplier, no route preference): D = N(E,R) - N(B,R) on hard328 lies near 0, in [-0.10, 0.07].

denials.why: The same claim on fresh2026: the edit has no route preference of its own beyond fewer slips, so its wrong answers are no nearer RL's than the cued base's are once each model's own wrong-answer concentration is normalized out.
denials.instead: S3: D_fresh = N(E,R) - N(B,R) lies near 0, in [-0.10, 0.07].
